theory.text: Theory only goes so far. Here's the same goal, written two ways. Read both, then notice what's actually different — not just longer, but more decided.

bad.label: Vague
bad.content: Build me a CRM for real estate agents.

good.label: Specific
good.content: Build a CRM for real estate agents. Two roles: agents (manage their own leads) and managers (see all leads). Lead has: name, phone, email, status (new/contacted/showing/closed/lost), assigned agent, notes, source. Stack: Next.js + Supabase + Tailwind. Auth: magic link. Show leads in a kanban grouped by status.

theory.text: The vague version forces the AI to guess on every dimension: schema, auth, UI pattern, stack. Some guesses will be wrong, and you'll spend an hour undoing them. The specific version locks the boring decisions and frees the AI to do the actual work — generating clean, well-structured code that matches what you wanted.
Specificity isn't bureaucracy. Every decision you don't make, the AI makes for you — and you'll have to live with it.

exercise.prompt_template: A [BLANK] prompt forces the AI to guess; a [BLANK] prompt locks the boring decisions so it can focus on building.

blanks.hint_2: It's the kind that fits in one sentence with no concrete fields or stack.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'vague' (or 'generic'). Vague prompts produce generic output — and the AI's defaults are rarely yours.

blanks.hint_1: The opposite of vague — what is it?
blanks.hint_2: It names roles, fields, stack, expected behavior.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'specific' (or 'detailed'). Specific prompts get specific code that actually fits your project.

outro.recap: You saw the difference: vague prompts force guesses, specific prompts unlock real work.
outro.next_prompt: Next: when one prompt isn't enough — chaining for complex features.
